general_conventions: B marks are independent marks awarded only when the specific point is seen in the answer.
M marks are method marks; if an M mark is not scored, the A marks that depend on it cannot be scored.
C marks are compensatory method marks: they can be awarded even if the equation/step is not written, provided later correct working shows it was known.
A marks are accuracy/answer marks that depend on an M mark or allow C marks to be scored; A0 in a 'show that' means the given value earns no mark itself.
ECF (error carried forward): a wrong earlier answer used correctly later is not penalised again.
AW = alternative wording accepted; ORA = or reverse argument; '/' separates alternative acceptable answers; words in brackets are not essential; underlined words must be present.
'reject'/'not' = answers not worthy of credit; 'ignore' = irrelevant statements that neither gain nor lose credit; 'allow' = acceptable answers.

Annotations used include BOD (benefit of doubt), CON (contradiction), ECF, L1/L2/L3 (levels), TE (transcription error), POT (power-of-ten error), SF (significant figure error), WP (wrong physics or equation).
Significant figures: if data are given to 2 s.f., answers to 2 or more s.f. are allowed; an answer to fewer than 2 s.f. is penalised once only in the whole paper unless guidance says otherwise.

Level of Response (asterisked, 6-mark) questions are 5(b) and 7(a): read the whole answer, choose the best-fit level, then award the higher mark in the level for a good match including the communication statement, or the lower mark where there are key omissions in content or communication.
Crossed-out work is not marked if an alternative is given; a crossed-out whole answer with no replacement is still marked.
NR (no response) is used for blank answers or irrelevant comments; 0 marks is given for an attempt that earns no credit (including copying the question).
Annotations listed: DO NOT ALLOW, IGNORE, ALLOW, brackets for non-essential words, underlining for essential words, ECF, AW, ORA.
Alternative correct answers and unexpected approaches must be credited fairly.

questions.context: Why the wire's vertical force on the rod is half the sign's weight.
questions.answer: Moments about the wall pivot: W acts at l/2, wire's vertical component at l, so F = W/2 = 60 N.
marking_points: B1: take moments about the rod–wall contact (removes unknown wall force)
B1: W × l/2 = F × l, i.e. F acts at twice the distance of W
pitfalls: Saying 'the wire takes half the weight' without moment reasoning

questions.context: Tension in wire at 30° to rod given vertical component 60 N.
Arrow for the wall's force on the rod.
questions.answer: Arrow from rod–wall junction through the point where T and line of W cross.
marking_points: B1: arrow from junction through intersection of T and W lines of action

questions.context: How the direction of the wall force was chosen.
questions.answer: Three forces in equilibrium must pass through one point / form closed triangle.
marking_points: B1: forces must form a closed triangle / pass through a common point for equilibrium

Compare landing velocities of two trajectories and choose one for longer roll on the green.
questions.answer: Same speed (17 m s^-1), different angles (60° vs 30°); 30° has larger horizontal velocity so likely rolls further.

B1: sensible choice with reason, e.g. larger horizontal velocity (30°) travels further, or higher bounce (60°) with less grass drag
allow_reject_ignore: Accept any sensible answer e.g. steeper impact loses more energy

questions.context: Design LDR light-meter circuit whose reading rises with light; explain and choose fixed resistor for largest change.
questions.answer: LDR in series with fixed resistor; voltmeter across resistor (or ammeter in series); light up → R(LDR) down → reading up; 750 Ω gives largest change.
marking_points: L3 (5-6): circuit with meter correctly drawn, action correctly explained, sensitivity understood and 750 Ω justified (6); LDR symbol wrong or resistor not fully justified (5)
L2 (3-4): correct LDR symbol, limited action explanation, 750 Ω stated not justified (4); any point omitted/incorrect (3)
L1 (1-2): correct LDR symbol (1); action addresses one point (1); sensitivity poorly addressed (1); max 2
Circuit: resistor and LDR in series; ammeter in series or voltmeter across fixed resistor; correct symbols
Action: light up → LDR resistance falls → current rises / pd across resistor rises (pd across LDR falls) → meter reading rises
Sensitivity: need the largest change in current or pd for a given change in light; choose 750 Ω (comparable to the LDR range) for largest meter change
pitfalls: Voltmeter across LDR (reading falls as light increases)

questions.context: Speed of sound from two successive resonance lengths at 500 Hz, with reasoning.
marking_points: B1: tube moved λ/2 between resonances (or antinode at open end, node at water)
allow_reject_ignore: Solution worked to 2 s.f. scores max 3
pitfalls: Using l1 = λ/4 directly (ignores end correction)

questions.context: Whether using 5000 Hz would give a more or less accurate speed of sound.
questions.answer: Less accurate: smaller wavelength gives shorter lengths, larger percentage uncertainty.
marking_points: B1: smaller λ means smaller lengths measured, so less accurate
B1: added detail/expansion (e.g. larger percentage uncertainty for same ruler resolution)
pitfalls: Claiming higher frequency is always more accurate

questions.context: How and when a stationary wave forms in a pipe; compare air molecule motion at P (λ/4 from end) and Q (end).
questions.answer: Reflected wave superposes with incident wave giving nodes/antinodes; antinodes at both open ends (L = nλ/2); Q antinode: max-amplitude oscillation along axis; P node: no motion.
marking_points: B1: wave reflected at end superposes/interferes with incident wave
B1: resultant has nodes and antinodes
B1: both ends antinodes / pipe length nλ/2
B1: at Q air molecules oscillate
B1: along the tube axis with maximum amplitude

questions.context: How to use an LED circuit to find accurate Vmin values and use data graphically to find h.
questions.answer: Raise pd from zero until each LED just strikes (shielded), repeat and average; plot Vmin vs 1/λ through origin; gradient = hc/e, h = e × gradient/c.
marking_points: L3 (5-6): at least experiment points 3, 4 and 2 or 5, plus processing points 1, 2 and 5; well-developed logical reasoning
L1 (1-2): at least 2 experiment + 1 processing point or vice versa

Experiment: set potential divider to low/zero pd; connect lead to one LED; increase pd until LED just lights; repeat several times and average Vmin; repeat for each LED; shield LED in opaque tube to judge switch-on
Processing: Vmin against 1/λ is a straight line; through origin; calculate 1/λ values; best-fit line through origin; gradient G = Vmin λ = hc/e; h = eG/c
pitfalls: No method to judge switch-on accurately

questions.context: Why the KEmax–frequency graph cannot be explained by wave model.

B1: nor why electron KE depends on frequency (not intensity)
